html:
An ancient Greek city in eastern Libya, near today's Shahhat, founded about 631 BCE by settlers from Thera. It was the leading city of the region that took its name, Cyrenaica, and the head of a group of five cities called the Pentapolis.

It stood on a high green plateau a few miles from the sea, with good farmland and pasture. Its wealth came from grain, horses and above all silphium, a plant prized as a medicine and spice that was harvested to extinction in Roman times. Its temples of Apollo and Zeus rivalled those of Greece.

Cyrene was ruled by its own kings, then by Ptolemaic Egypt, and from 96 BCE by Rome. It produced the philosopher Aristippus, the poet Callimachus and the scholar Eratosthenes. A Jewish revolt in 115 CE and the earthquake of 365 left it badly damaged, and it slowly faded. Its ruins are a World Heritage Site. For how it was founded see Greeks found Cyrene.
